title: Winded Migration
full_review:
The spectacular documentary "Winged Migration" (Sony Classics) elicits awe at God's perfection in his creations. With minimal dialogue and exhilarating cinematography, director and narrator Jacques Perrin's quietly thrilling film provides a heady vicarious experience as it captures the migratory patterns of birds.

But this is not your ordinary nature film. "Winged Migration" transcends the genre to become a most astounding piece of work. In this Oscar-nominated film, the French director and his teams of filmmakers spent three years traveling through 40 countries and all seven continents capturing the winged wonders as they traveled sometimes more than 10,000 miles between the tropics and the Arctic to ensure their survival.

Nature is the special effect here. The stupendous camera work makes it feel like the viewer has joined the flock of cranes or storks as they pierce the skies, floating high above the clouds to reach their destination. The tender close-up of a mother bird feeding her newly-hatched chicks is just as breathtaking as a shot of thousands of tiny feathered ones filling up the screen like a fast-moving black cloud. The editing is crisp and precise, knowing just when to cut away as a tractor closes in on a fledgling that has made its home deep in the sheaves of wheat.
To say the film is escapist fare is to trivialize the wonder and beauty of it -- but one does get lost in it. The score by Bruno Coulais is an ethereal combination of chanting, pulsating beats and folksy rhythms, alternately emphasizing the urgency of the creatures' life-and-death search for food or their slower tempo when it comes to family time.

Entertaining as well as educational for all in the family, "Winged Migration" also has a philosophical frame to it. Questions about man vs. nature, human beings' responsibility in caring for the Earth, and God's role in the cycle of life and death come to mind. If God cared enough to create creatures that instinctively know how to travel from one end of the Earth to the other, how much more are we, as human beings made in God's image, capable of? Older children in the family may enjoy engaging in such discussions.

Uplifting the spirit, "Winged Migration" helps the viewer appreciate nature's awesome power and maybe even feel a little closer to God.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences.
